subject: Polity
description: Covers 73rd Amendment and State Election Commission.

questions.stem: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, added which new Part and Schedule to the Indian Constitution to constitutionalize the Panchayati Raj Institutions?

options.option_text: Part IX and the 11th Schedule
Part IX-A and the 12th Schedule
Part VIII and the 10th Schedule
Part X and the 9th Schedule

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The historic 73rd Amendment Act breathed life into Article 40 (a DPSP instructing the state to organize village panchayats). It added a new Part IX titled "The Panchayats" and the 11th Schedule, which contains 29 functional items (like agriculture, rural housing, roads) that State Legislatures can devolve to Panchayats.
DECOY BUSTING: 
- Part IX-A and the 12th Schedule were added by the 74th Amendment for Municipalities (Urban Local Bodies).
- The 10th Schedule is the Anti-Defection Law. 
- The 9th Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment to protect land reforms from judicial review.
EXAM INSIGHT: The Act mandates a 3-tier system (Village, Intermediate/Block, and District levels) for all states having a population above 20 lakhs. It also mandates reserving exactly 1/3rd of all seats for women, a revolutionary step for rural political empowerment.

questions.stem: Under the 73rd Amendment, which constitutional body is explicitly created to conduct free and fair elections strictly for the Panchayats and Municipalities?

options.option_text: The State Election Commission
The Election Commission of India
The Delimitation Commission
The State Public Service Commission

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Article 243K mandates the creation of a State Election Commission (SEC) in every state. The SEC consists of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor. The sole responsibility of the SEC is the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to the Panchayats (and Municipalities).
DECOY BUSTING: The central Election Commission of India (ECI) conducts elections ONLY for the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Assemblies, President, and Vice-President. The ECI has absolutely no role in Panchayat elections.
EXAM INSIGHT: To ensure independence, the State Election Commissioner can only be removed from office in the exact same manner and on the exact same grounds as a Judge of a High Court (proving misbehavior or incapacity through parliamentary impeachment), not at the mere pleasure of the Governor.

questions.stem: Article 243(b) of the Constitution defines 'Gram Sabha' as a body consisting of which of the following persons?

options.option_text: Elected ward members of the Gram Panchayat executive
Persons enrolled in the electoral roll of the Panchayat village
All adult residents living within the revenue village boundary
Members nominated by the concerned Block Development Officer

questions.explanation: Article 243(b) defines Gram Sabha as persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village within the Panchayat area — i.e., enrolled voters, not all residents. Option C is wrong because residency alone does not confer Gram Sabha membership; only registered voters qualify. Option A confuses the Gram Sabha (the general body) with the Gram Panchayat (the elected executive body).

questions.stem: Article 243D of the Constitution mandates reservation of seats for women in Panchayati Raj institutions. What is the minimum fraction reserved for women across all tiers?

options.option_text: One-fourth of the total number of seats to be filled
One-half of the total number of seats to be filled
Two-fifths of the total number of seats to be filled
One-third of the total number of seats to be filled

questions.explanation: Article 243D(3) mandates that not less than one-third of the total seats in each Panchayat shall be reserved for women, applicable at all three tiers. This reservation extends to offices of Chairpersons as well under Article 243D(4). Several states have raised this to 50% by state law, but the constitutional floor is one-third. Option B (one-half) reflects state-level enhancements, not the constitutional minimum.

questions.stem: The Eleventh Schedule, inserted by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, enumerates subjects that may be devolved to Panchayats. How many such functional items does it contain?

options.option_text: 29 items ranging from agriculture to public distribution systems
18 items covering agriculture and allied rural activities only
24 items spanning rural development and elementary education
34 items including forestry, environment and land acquisition

questions.explanation: The Eleventh Schedule contains exactly 29 subjects, including agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, animal husbandry, fisheries, social forestry, primary and secondary education, women and child development, poverty alleviation, and public distribution systems. 18 is the number sometimes confused with entries in another context; 34 is a distractor inflated beyond the actual list. Devolution of these subjects to Panchayats is discretionary for states, not mandatory.

questions.stem: Which Article of the Constitution directs the Governor of a state to constitute a Finance Commission to review the financial position of Panchayats at intervals of five years?

options.option_text: Article 243-G (powers and functions conferred on Panchayats)
Article 243-H (Panchayat authority to levy taxes and fees)
Article 243-I (State Finance Commission for Panchayats)
Article 243-J (audit of accounts of Panchayati Raj bodies)

questions.explanation: Article 243-I mandates that the Governor shall constitute a Finance Commission within one year of the 73rd Amendment's commencement and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year, to review the financial position of Panchayats and make recommendations on tax devolution and grants-in-aid. Article 243-G is commonly confused here as it deals with functional devolution, not financial review. The State Finance Commission under 243-I is distinct from the Central Finance Commission under Article 280.

questions.stem: Which study team, appointed in 1957 by the National Development Council, first recommended the creation of a three-tier Panchayati Raj structure at the village, block, and district levels?

options.option_text: Ashok Mehta Committee (recommended consolidating into two tiers)
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (pioneered the three-tier model)
G.V.K. Rao Committee (described Panchayats as a paperless tiger)
L.M. Singhvi Committee (recommended constitutional protection for Panchayats)

questions.explanation: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended democratic decentralisation through a three-tier structure: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block), and Zila Parishad (district). Rajasthan was the first state to implement it in 1959. Option A is wrong because the Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) actually recommended a two-tier structure. Option C (G.V.K. Rao, 1985) diagnosed the decay of Panchayati Raj, coining 'grass without roots'. Option D (L.M. Singhvi, 1986) recommended giving Panchayats constitutional status.

questions.stem: Under Article 243B(2) of the Constitution, a state is not required to constitute Panchayats at the intermediate level if its total population does not exceed a specific threshold. What is that threshold?

options.option_text: Fifteen lakh persons as specified in the constitutional text
Twenty-five lakh persons as specified in the constitutional text
Twenty lakh persons as specified in the constitutional text
Thirty lakh persons as specified in the constitutional text

questions.explanation: Article 243B(2) explicitly provides that a state with a population not exceeding twenty lakhs need not constitute Panchayats at the intermediate level, allowing a two-tier structure instead of the standard three-tier one. This provision accommodates smaller states like Goa and some north-eastern states. Twenty-five lakh is a common distractor; the precise constitutional figure is twenty lakh. Confusing this with the quorum threshold or election trigger conditions is a frequent error.

questions.stem: The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends Part IX of the Constitution to Fifth Schedule tribal areas. Under which constitutional provision does Parliament derive express authority to enact PESA?

options.option_text: Article 244A, which empowers creation of autonomous states in tribal regions
Article 275(1), which authorises special grants to states for tribal welfare
Article 243M(4)(b), empowering Parliament to extend Part IX to Scheduled Areas
Article 371, containing special provisions for certain north-eastern states

questions.explanation: Article 243M(1) excludes Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule) from the automatic application of Part IX. However, Article 243M(4)(b) carves out an exception: where the State Legislature has not extended Part IX to its Scheduled Areas, Parliament may by law do so with such exceptions and modifications as it specifies. PESA 1996 is exactly that law. Option A (Article 244A) relates to formation of an autonomous state within Assam for tribal areas and is unrelated to PESA. Article 275(1) deals only with financial grants, not legislative extension of Panchayati Raj.
